title: Acute cholecystitis and acute cholangitis
subject: surgery-trauma
setting: Emergency department, surgical ward, ICU, endoscopy
summary: Diagnose and grade severity with the Tokyo Guidelines 2018, resuscitate and start antibiotics, perform early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 7 days of admission and 10 days of symptoms) for cholecystitis, and arrange biliary drainage, usually ERCP, timed to cholangitis severity.

sections.title: Diagnosis (Tokyo Guidelines 2018)
items: Acute cholecystitis: A local signs (Murphy sign, RUQ pain, mass or tenderness); B systemic signs (fever, raised CRP, raised WBC); C imaging findings of cholecystitis. Suspected: one A plus one B. Definite: A plus B plus C.

Acute cholangitis: A inflammation (fever above 38°C or rigors; WBC below 4000 or above 10,000 per microlitre, or CRP 1 mg/dL or more); B cholestasis (bilirubin 2 mg/dL or more, or ALP, GGT, AST or ALT above 1.5 times the upper limit); C imaging (biliary dilatation, or a stone, stricture or stent).
Cholangitis is suspected with one A item plus one B or C item, and definite with one item each from A, B and C. Charcot triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) is specific but insensitive.
Reynolds pentad (Charcot triad plus shock and confusion) signals severe cholangitis needing urgent drainage.

sections.title: Investigations
items: FBC, CRP, bilirubin, ALP, GGT, AST, ALT, lipase or amylase, creatinine, electrolytes, coagulation, lactate, and 2 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics in suspected cholangitis.

Abdominal ultrasound first (gallstones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign, duct dilatation). HIDA scan is the most accurate test if doubt remains; CT is poor for cholecystitis itself but useful for complications and other diagnoses.

Stratify common bile duct stone risk with LFTs and ultrasound: MRCP, EUS, intraoperative cholangiography or laparoscopic ultrasound for intermediate risk; ERCP, intraoperative cholangiography or laparoscopic ultrasound for high risk. Raised LFTs alone do not prove a duct stone.
In northern and eastern India, gallbladder cancer is common: look for irregular wall thickening, a mass, or liver invasion on imaging.

sections.title: Acute cholecystitis
items: Severity (TG18): Grade III with any organ dysfunction (vasopressor need, reduced consciousness, PaO2/FiO2 below 300, oliguria or creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL, INR above 1.5, platelets below 100,000 per microlitre); Grade II with WBC above 18,000, palpable tender RUQ mass, symptoms over 72 hours, or marked local inflammation (gangrene, abscess, emphysematous, biliary peritonitis); otherwise Grade I.

Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy as soon as possible, within 7 days of admission and 10 days of symptom onset, when surgical expertise is available (WSES 2020); this includes patients over 80, Child-Pugh A and B cirrhosis, and pregnancy.
If early surgery is not possible, delay cholecystectomy until after 6 weeks. Avoid surgery in septic shock or with absolute anaesthetic contraindications.
Patients unfit for surgery: gallbladder drainage (percutaneous cholecystostomy, or endoscopic transpapillary or EUS-guided drainage in expert centres).
Difficult anatomy: subtotal cholecystectomy or conversion to open surgery rather than risking bile duct injury.
Antibiotics: none after cholecystectomy for uncomplicated cholecystitis; 4 to 7 days after source control for gangrenous, emphysematous or perforated gallbladder.

sections.title: Acute cholangitis
items: Severity (TG18): Grade III with any organ dysfunction (as for cholecystitis); Grade II with any 2 of WBC above 12,000 or below 4000 per microlitre, fever 39°C or more, age 75 or more, bilirubin 5 mg/dL or more, albumin below 0.7 times the lower limit of normal; otherwise Grade I.

Grade I: antibiotics and supportive care; drain if there is no response within 24 hours. Grade II: early biliary drainage with antibiotics. Grade III: organ support and urgent biliary drainage as soon as the patient is stabilised.

ERCP with stent or sphincterotomy is first choice; percutaneous transhepatic drainage if ERCP fails or anatomy is altered. In unstable patients place a stent or nasobiliary drain and defer complete stone clearance. Many guidelines (for example ASGE 2021) favour ERCP within 48 hours.
After gallstone cholangitis settles, plan cholecystectomy (ideally in the same admission) to prevent recurrence.

sections.title: Antibiotics (adapt to local antibiogram)
items: Send blood cultures, and bile cultures at drainage. Start antibiotics promptly: within 1 hour in septic shock.

Community-acquired Grade I or II: ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily (add metronidazole 500 mg IV every 8 hours if there is a biliary-enteric anastomosis), or amoxicillin-clavulanate if local resistance is low.

Grade III, healthcare-associated, or high ESBL prevalence (common in Indian hospitals): piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours or meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours; add vancomycin in Grade III or healthcare-associated infection to cover Enterococcus.
Duration: cholangitis 4 to 7 days after source control; at least 2 weeks for Enterococcus or Streptococcus bacteraemia. De-escalate by culture results.

sections.title: Escalate
items: ICU for Grade III disease, persistent hypotension or rising lactate after fluids.
Urgent endoscopy or interventional radiology for cholangitis not responding to antibiotics within 24 hours, or immediately if in shock.
Transfer if ERCP or percutaneous drainage is unavailable locally and the patient has Grade II or III cholangitis.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating cholangitis with antibiotics alone while delaying drainage.
Diagnosing a duct stone on LFTs alone, or missing one before cholecystectomy.
Discharging after conservative treatment without planned cholecystectomy, leading to recurrent attacks.
Underestimating gangrenous or perforated cholecystitis in diabetic and older patients with few signs.
Continuing antibiotics for days after an uncomplicated cholecystectomy.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.notes: Grade I and II community-acquired biliary infection.

drugs.name: Metronidazole
drugs.notes: Anaerobic cover; add when a biliary-enteric anastomosis is present.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.notes: Grade III or healthcare-associated; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.notes: ESBL risk or Grade III sepsis; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.dose: 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours, adjusted to levels
drugs.notes: Enterococcus cover in Grade III or healthcare-associated infection; adjust for renal function.
